title: Learning Lesson 8: It's Easy to Trick Yourself into Thinking You Know More Than You Know han-you-know
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This final installment of Dave Stuart Jr.'s eight-part Learning Lesson series, written as a script for delivering the lesson to students, covers the third and last of Stephen Chew's learning "pitfalls": that people are chronically overconfident about how well they understand material, especially when they've used passive study strategies like rereading or highlighting. Stuart explains that passive review creates a false sense of familiarity that gets mistaken for genuine understanding, and offers self-testing as the direct fix — because retrieval, unlike rereading, forces a student to discover in real time whether they actually know the material. He lists several concrete self-testing tactics (practice tests, teacher-provided SAQ patterns, end-of-chapter questions, peer-made test-question parties) students can use across their classes. The lesson closes the series by tying self-testing back to overlearning: the act of testing yourself is itself a mechanism for making knowledge automatic, addressing several of the bottlenecks and pitfalls covered earlier in the series. In a closing note to teachers, Stuart argues that explicitly teaching students how learning works is necessary to unlock the Effort and Efficacy beliefs that underlie student motivation.
points: Passive study strategies like rereading and highlighting don't just fail to build understanding — they actively produce a false sense of mastery, which is the mechanism behind chronic learner overconfidence.
Self-testing is presented as the single fix for overconfidence because it forces real-time, honest feedback about what a student does and doesn't actually know, unlike passive review.

Stuart gives teachers concrete self-testing formats to hand students: practice tests, teacher-shared question patterns (like his own SAQ approach), end-of-chapter questions, and peer-generated "test question parties."

Self-testing does double duty — beyond correcting overconfidence, the retrieval act itself is a mechanism for overlearning, connecting this pitfall back to the concentration and forgetting bottlenecks covered earlier in the series.
quotes: Folks are often OVERCONFIDENT when judging how well they understand something. Let's get that down.

One reason that's true is because those are passive strategies — they don't require much effort, and they don't really require you to understand anything. But another reason is that they make you overconfident.
The way to fix this overconfidence really quickly is to test yourself! All right — so, how can we test ourselves?
The only way to know if you know something is to test yourself. And what's cool is that the act of testing yourself is actually a good method for overlearning material and making it automatic.
There's no way to have an optimally motivated class of learners who have not had a chance to learn more about learning in that class. We gotta teach 'em how to advance toward mastery.
